sourceDescriptionRaw:
Preschool age children and their parents/caregivers are invited to the West Valley Branch Library for Reading to Children in Japanese. Every Thursday at 11:00 AM, children will enjoy early literacy activities such as stories, songs, rhymes, fingerplays, and movement activities all in the Japanese language. 
This program is brought to the library by Poponta Children's Cultural Society. Established in 2008 and based in San Mateo, Poponta is comprised of a group of volunteers dedicated to serving the Japanese-speaking community. Poponta volunteers tell stories to children to open their minds to the magic of books. To learn more about Poponta, please visit:nbsp;https://ja-jp.facebook.com/popontanokai/
Free, with limited capacity. Seating is available on a first-come, first-served basis. A limited number of tickets will be distributed at the Information Desk 30 minutes prior to the start of the program. San José Public Library Early Education programs are in alignment with the City’s Education and Digital Literacy Initiative. 
 
ADA Accommodation Requests

title: Making Letters: Typography Across Hand, Screen, and Loom
description: Beginning with hand-lettered high school book covers and the construction of letterforms with gouache and a ruling pen in college, she follows this trajectory through professional art direction and digital typesetting, original typeface design, and her recent project of weaving the alphabet.
parentSummary: Beginning with hand-lettered high school book covers and the construction of letterforms with gouache and a ruling pen in college, she follows this trajectory through professional art direction and digital typesetting, original typeface design, and her recent project of weaving the alphabet.
sourceDescriptionRaw: RSVP Link: HTTPS://TINYURL.COM/STSAMY26 How do the tools used to create letterforms shape the way those forms are imagined, constructed, and understood? In this presentation, graphic designer, educator, type designer, and fiber artist Amy Copeland traces her evolving relationship with typography across analog, digital, and textile practices. Beginning with hand-lettered high school book covers and the construction of letterforms with gouache and a ruling pen in college, she follows this trajectory through professional art direction and digital typesetting, original typeface design, and her recent project of weaving the alphabet. Through this practice-based account, Copeland considers how typographic knowledge moves between technologies and materials. Digital tools make letterforms reproducible, scalable, and precisely adjustable; weaving translates those same forms into physical structures governed by warp, weft, tension, sequence, and touch. These material constraints do more than alter the appearance of a letter—they influence how it is conceived and constructed.Rather than treating analog and digital processes as opposites, Copeland explores the productive exchange between them. Her work demonstrates how knowledge gained through one form of making can migrate into another, revealing letters not as fixed symbols but as adaptable structures shaped by tools, materials, and embodied experience. ---------- Amy Copeland loves to make things. A graphic designer and educator for more than 30 years, she brings her interest in typography and letterforms to her weaving practice. She recently completed a woven alphabet and also creates tapestries and rugs using geometric shapes and patterns. Her work has been exhibited at Worthington Yards in Cleveland, Lakeland Community College, Cyrus Gallery, Malone College Art Gallery, and the McDonough Museum of Art at Youngstown State University. Copeland is an Assistant Professor of Graphic + Interactive Design at Youngstown State University. She holds a BS in Graphic Design from the University of Cincinnati, an MFA in Visual Communication Design, and an MS in User Experience Design from Kent State University. She recently earned a postgraduate certificate in type design through the Type West program at Letterform Archive.

title: Master Gardeners: The Thrifty Table: Creating Beautiful Holiday Centerpieces
description: You’ll Learn: \nThe Art of the “Found” Object: Learn how to scout your own backyard or junk drawer for unique textures, greenery, and accents that add character to any arrangement.Grocery Store Glam: Discover how to deconstruct those affordable supermarket flower bunches and reimagine them into high-end-looking centerpieces.
parentSummary: You’ll Learn: \nThe Art of the “Found” Object: Learn how to scout your own backyard or junk drawer for unique textures, greenery, and accents that add character to any arrangement.Grocery Store Glam: Discover how to deconstruct those affordable supermarket flower bunches and reimagine them into high-end-looking centerpieces.
sourceDescriptionRaw:
Join a Santa Clara County Master Gardener for a monthly talk on various topics.This month:nbsp;Are you experiencing the “holiday guest stress syndrome”? Don’t let the pressure of having a perfect tablescape wilt your holiday spirit!
Join UC Master Gardeners Laura Westley and Bernie Day for an inspiring, hands-on demonstration designed to take the stress—and the high cost—out of holiday decorating. You don’t need a professional florist or a massive budget to create a “wow” factor for your dining room.
What You’ll Learn: 
The Art of the “Found” Object: Learn how to scout your own backyard or junk drawer for unique textures, greenery, and accents that add character to any arrangement.Grocery Store Glam: Discover how to deconstruct those affordable supermarket flower bunches and reimagine them into high-end-looking centerpieces.Pro-Tips for Longevity: Get the inside scoop on keeping your flora fresh from the first toast to the final slice of pie. 
Why join us? Whether you’re hosting a grand feast or an intimate gathering, you’ll walk away with the confidence and practical skills to transform “ordinary” items into extraordinary focal points.
Upcoming topics are:November 14 - The Thrifty Table: Creating Beautiful Holiday Centerpieces.- no talk in December -
Detailed program descriptions to be updated when available.
Free. No registration required.ADA Accommodation Requests

title: Documentaries: Holodomor Remembrance Day
description: Through compelling eyewitness accounts, the film brings into focus a pivotal and little-known period in history, the consequences of which continues to reverberate today.\nBooks on this reading listnbsp;will be on display and available.\nRegistration is not necessary, but registering means you will receive a reminder email the day before.
parentSummary: Through compelling eyewitness accounts, the film brings into focus a pivotal and little-known period in history, the consequences of which continues to reverberate today.\nBooks on this reading listnbsp;will be on display and available.\nRegistration is not necessary, but registering means you will receive a reminder email the day before.
sourceDescriptionRaw:
The Holodomor, the faminenbsp;that killed millions of Ukrainians in the 1930s, was not widely known or acknowledged until the fall of the Soviet Union in the 1990s.nbsp;Established in 1998,nbsp;Holodomor Remembrance Day is observed on the fourth Saturday of November to remember the one-quarter of Ukraine's population who died during the Holodomor.nbsp;
Join us for Palo Alto City Library's second annualnbsp;program commemorating this event and its lasting effects fornbsp;some in our community today. Three short documentaries will give us the historicalnbsp;background that reverberates innbsp;current events.nbsp;Descriptions of the documentariesnbsp;below were written by their creators.
Holodomor: How Millions of Ukrainians Died of Starvation During Stalin-Era Mass Famine (Radio Free Europe, 2019, two minutes).nbsp;Each year, on the fourth Saturday of November, Ukraine remembers the millions who died during the Holodomor, the Stalin-era famine that devastated the population in 1932-1933. Many countries consider it to have been genocide.Minnesota Memories of the Holodomornbsp;(PBS, 2025, 26 minutes).nbsp;In an extraordinary exploration of the transmission of traumatic memory within families, communities and across generations, Ukrainians in Minneapolis-St. Paul share their family stories about the Holodomor artificial famine of 1932-33 and the local community's efforts to come to terms with genocide, even as war once again threatens the existence of Ukrainians as a people. Holodomor: Voices of Survivors (2015, 30 minutes).nbsp;Twenty-five Ukrainian Canadians tell their stories of survival during the Holodomor--death inflicted by starvation--a genocide of Ukrainian people engineered by Joseph Stalin during 1932 and 1933. Through compelling eyewitness accounts, the film brings into focus a pivotal and little-known period in history, the consequences of which continues to reverberate today.
Books on this reading listnbsp;will be on display and available.
Registration is not necessary, but registering means you will receive a reminder email the day before.

description: Everyone is welcome to attend and listen ornbsp;read poetry and join in related discussions.nbsp;Meetings are onnbsp;the second Saturday of everynbsp;month, no registration needed.nbsp;\nThe Garlicky Group of Poetsnbsp;has been hosted by the Gilroy Librarynbsp;since 1995.nbsp; These monthly readings attract residents from throughout South County.

sourceDescriptionRaw:
Everyone is welcome to attend and listen ornbsp;read poetry and join in related discussions.nbsp;Meetings are onnbsp;the second Saturday of everynbsp;month, no registration needed.nbsp;
The Garlicky Group of Poetsnbsp;has been hosted by the Gilroy Librarynbsp;since 1995.nbsp; These monthly readings attract residents from throughout South County. Ed Nauss founded the readings whichnbsp;are free and open to all, not just poets. “Procedures are relaxed, informal, providing equal opportunity for all,” he said. “There is never a ‘featured’ reader, nor is there any internal competition. title: Tidal Marsh Appreciation

parentSummary: Join Docent Naturalists Susan Bernhard, Ann Reisenauer, and Alison Hurst to explore the flora, fauna, and environmental issues of the salt marshes on this leisurely-paced, family-friendly walk along the Bay Trail.
sourceDescriptionRaw: Tidal salt marshes flood twice each day. They provide critical habitat for marine invertebrates such as oysters, mussels, and clams, shorebirds, and specialized native plants like pickleweed. Additionally, the baylands are on the Pacific Flyway, the great bird migration route between Alaska and South America. But wetlands are easy to overlook, often underappreciated, and threatened by climate change. Join Docent Naturalists Susan Bernhard, Ann Reisenauer, and Alison Hurst to explore the flora, fauna, and environmental issues of the salt marshes on this leisurely-paced, family-friendly walk along the Bay Trail.

sourceDescriptionRaw:
In collaboration with JMM Dance Co., Gilroy Library is hosting monthly Inclusive Sensory Movement and Regulation workshops every third Sunday for the rest of 2026.nbsp;
These workshops will introduce families to sensory regulation through gentle, structurednbsp;movement activities grounded in rhythm, body awareness, and emotional safety. Led bynbsp;trained JMM Dance Co. facilitators, children are invited to participate at their own comfortnbsp;level—moving, observing, or resting as needed.nbsp;Activities are designed to support self-regulation, confidence, and connection withoutnbsp;pressure to perform, making the experience accessible for children with autism and othernbsp;sensory processing differences.
Registration is required for these workshops.nbsp;
Learn more about JMM Dance Co. and their work at their website here: JMM Dance Co.For accessibility accommodations (ex. ASL), please fill out the online form at sccld.org/accessibility 7+ days prior to the event. title: BYOB (Bring Your Own Book) Book Club
description: Find a book that is funny, witty, or clever with themes such as dark humor, satire, or comedic reliefMay 20: Movie Adaptation May!
parentSummary: Find a book that is funny, witty, or clever with themes such as dark humor, satire, or comedic reliefMay 20: Movie Adaptation May!
sourceDescriptionRaw:
Bring a book that you have read that fits into our monthly theme.
Come for recommendations, reviews and rapport.
We meet in person at the Joyce Ellington Library. 
Please join us for an afternoon of literary discussion! 
All are welcome! 
Upcoming Book Themes:
January 28: New Year, New You!: Kick off the new year with a book to inspire or motivate you. Discover a new hobby, dive into a self-help book, or explore health and fitness.
February 25: Romance: Fall in love with a classic romance novel or discover a new romantasy author.
March 25:nbsp;Spring Cleaning! Clean out your bookshelf and read a book you have been meaning to read but haven't yet or rediscover a book you may have forgotten about.
April 29:nbsp;Comedy! Find a book that is funny, witty, or clever with themes such as dark humor, satire, or comedic reliefMay 20: Movie Adaptation May! Read a book that has been adapted into a movie, pick an old favorite, or a book with a movie coming to theatres soon.
June 24:nbsp;Pride Month. Focus on diverse LGBTQIA+ experiences through contemporary fiction, queer classics, or genre-bending stories.
July 22: Graphic Novel Month. Read a manga, graphic novel or comic book. Try a new genre or read a graphic novel that illustrates an old classic.
August 26: Beach Reads. Embrace summer reading with a book you would read on the beach or by the pool.
September 30: Sci-Fi September. Transition to the “spooky season” with sci-fi reads including apocalyptic, cyberpunk, dystopian, time travel, and more.
October 28: Horror/Gothic literature. Explore the dark side of literature with a contemporary, supernatural or gothic tale. 
November 18: Non-fiction November. Dive into nonfiction and select a true story, memoir or educational text. 
December 16: Best of 2026. Read a book that was published in 2026.
ADA Accommodation Requests

title: Intermediate Mass Black Holes; Meteor Showers or Space Debris?
description: In this talk, we explore how changes in visible gas emission lines over nearly two decades cannbsp;reveal these hidden engines, highlighting recent Magellan Spectrograph observations of dwarf galaxy J1143 that point to an accretingnbsp;intermediate-mass black hole at its core.
parentSummary: In this talk, we explore how changes in visible gas emission lines over nearly two decades cannbsp;reveal these hidden engines, highlighting recent Magellan Spectrograph observations of dwarf galaxy J1143 that point to an accretingnbsp;intermediate-mass black hole at its core.
sourceDescriptionRaw: Lecture 1:nbsp;nbsp;Understanding how supermassive black holes grow offers key clues to how galaxies evolve, but their "missing link"—intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs)—remains elusive. Because small, blue compact dwarf galaxies cannot host supermassive monsters, theynbsp;are prime hunting grounds for IMBHs. In this talk, we explore how changes in visible gas emission lines over nearly two decades cannbsp;reveal these hidden engines, highlighting recent Magellan Spectrograph observations of dwarf galaxy J1143 that point to an accretingnbsp;intermediate-mass black hole at its core. Delivered by Kiera Aston.\nLecture 2:nbsp;nbsp;Gorgeous meteor showers streaking across the zenith, or space trash entering our atmosphere? The 21st century’s growing “spacenbsp;environment” problem is beginning to take center stage. Space debris, artificial spacecraft and objects that have ceased functioning,nbsp;are accumulating in Low Earth Orbit at an unprecedented rate. We are developing a global space debris monitoring network usingnbsp;ground-based observations. At the core of the system is a three-channel multispectral camera designed to detect the aluminumnbsp;emission line in the near-UV spectrum, providing a distinctive signature for identifying space debris as it reenters Earth’s atmosphere.nbsp;Delivered by Alice Zou.\nFor accessibility accommodations (ex. ASL), please fill out the online form at sccld.org/accessibility 7+days prior to the event. If you need assistance with thenbsp;form, speak with a staff member at your local library, call (408) 540-3945, or email us at ask@lib.sccgov.org.

title: Beyond The Spotlight: One Life. Multiple Passions. Endless Possibilities.
description: \nThrough personal stories, practical insights, and thoughtful conversation, this event invites participants to rethink traditional career paths, make space for creativity, and redefine what success can look like.
parentSummary: \nThrough personal stories, practical insights, and thoughtful conversation, this event invites participants to rethink traditional career paths, make space for creativity, and redefine what success can look like.
sourceDescriptionRaw:
In this inspiring talk with professionals, we explore how passion for the performing arts can coexist with a primary career. Can you be a professional by day and a performer by choice? What does it look like when theater becomes more than a hobby without becoming your full-time profession?
Through personal stories, practical insights, and thoughtful conversation, this event invites participants to rethink traditional career paths, make space for creativity, and redefine what success can look like. We will discuss how aspiring performers can balance education, professional goals, personal responsibilities, and their love for the stage.
Join us for a thought-provoking discussion on pursuing Performing Arts and Theater as a Parallel Career Path: an exploration of passion, purpose, possibility, and the courage to embrace more than one professional identity.Carla PantojaCarla, born and raised in the South Bay, is an actor, fight director, teaching artist, intimacy director, and mom of two. She has been a Resident Artist of San Francisco Shakespeare Festival since 2014 and recently served as Director of Vision for the 2021 Free Shakespeare in the Park production of Pericles, Prince of Tyre, directing episodes 2 and 4. In 2020, she was in the acting company at Oregon Shakespeare Festival, returning in 2022 as the festival’s first female fight director. Carla is an associate instructor for Dueling Arts International and serves on their governing body as President. She is also a proud member of Making Good Trouble, an anti-racist training cohort based in the Bay Area. Carla has directed SF Shakes Shakespeare on Tour production of Romeo and Juliet and Comedy of Errors and Assistant Directed the 2017 Free Shakespeare in the Park production of Hamlet. She played Paulina in Free Shakespeare in the Park’s The Winter’s Tale, Tybalt in Romeo and Juliet, and Kate in The Taming of the Shrew. She’s performed with Cal Shakes, Shotgun Players, Crowded Fire, Playground, Lorraine Hansberry Theatre, and the SF Mime Troupe in the Bay Area to name a few.Vinay PandeVinay Pande is a Silicon Valley technology leader and a passionate theatre artist who brings together the worlds of innovation and performing arts. Originally from Mumbai, India, Vinay holds a degree in Instrumentation Engineering and began his career in telecommunications, where he was part of the core team that developed India’s first satellite-based mission-critical voice, data, and video network for the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO). He later worked as a researcher at the prestigious Bell Labs and holds 15 technology patents, and co-authored technical publications and books. Today, he serves as a Principal Architect at a leading technology company in Silicon Valley.
Beyond his technology career, Vinay has nurtured a deep passion for the performing arts for over a decade, actively pursuing theatre, acting, and singing across Marathi and Hindi productions. From bringing diverse characters to life on stage to engaging audiences as a Radio Jockey and event host, he thrives on the energy of live performance and the magic of storytelling. For Vinay, technology may be his profession, but the stage is where his creative spirit truly comes alive.Sowmya Renukuntla
Sowmya is a Bay Area native and recent graduate from Santa Clara University, where she studied Business and worked directly with Admission Counselors for four years. Since graduating, she has been working full-time at Levi Strauss Co. on the Corporate Insights team and is a part-time college counselor.Sponsored by the Cupertino Library Foundation.nbsp;For accessibility accommodations (ex. ASL), please fill out the online form at sccld.org/accessibility 7+ days prior to the event. If you need assistance with the form, speak with a staff member at your local library, call (408) 540-3945, or email us at ask@lib.sccgov.org.

You will learn about the songs, dances, art, food, and traditions of the Indigenous Peoples of America. Ohiya is a cultural collaboration of Native American Singers, Dancers and Artists from the greater San Francisco Bay Area. title: Festival of Lights: A Diwali Celebration
description: Noorani Dance, founded in 2016 by by international Kathak artist, Farah Yasmeen Shaikh, exemplifies Farah’s unique artistic expression and vision coupled with the classical and innovative influence and style of Farah's Guru, the late Pandit Chitresh Das.
parentSummary: Noorani Dance, founded in 2016 by by international Kathak artist, Farah Yasmeen Shaikh, exemplifies Farah’s unique artistic expression and vision coupled with the classical and innovative influence and style of Farah's Guru, the late Pandit Chitresh Das.
sourceDescriptionRaw: Join us at the Mitchell Park Community Center, as we celebrate Diwali! Enjoy fun activities for all ages including: Ongoing from 2-4 PM: Henna with teaching artist Rachel-Anne Palacios (Adobe Room; henna line closes at 3:30 PM!) Rangoli (chalk coloring craft outside in the Courtyard) Crafts (in Adobe Room) All activities available while supplies last! Performance from 2:30-3:30 PM in El Palo Alto Room by Noorani Dance. Rachel-Anne Palacios is an Afro-Chicana Oakland native, multi-cultural arts educator, and self-taught folk artist. She has been teaching art workshops and classes at Bay Area schools and libraries for over a decade and a half and her lessons and projects are inspired by indigenous cultures and traditional art from around the world. Noorani Dance, founded in 2016 by by international Kathak artist, Farah Yasmeen Shaikh, exemplifies Farah’s unique artistic expression and vision coupled with the classical and innovative influence and style of Farah's Guru, the late Pandit Chitresh Das. "Noorani" means bright or luminous, with a dual meaning of enlightenment. With Kathak dance as their medium, Noorani Dance is committed to enlightening minds and hearts through the arts.

title: My Very First Nutcracker
description: Kids will marvel at the historic San Jose Electric Light Tower rising magically above the streets of San Jose, and cheer on adorable mice and toy soldiers who compete to win a magic crown.
parentSummary: Kids will marvel at the historic San Jose Electric Light Tower rising magically above the streets of San Jose, and cheer on adorable mice and toy soldiers who compete to win a magic crown.
sourceDescriptionRaw: Sunday, December 20, 2026 at 11 a.m. Tuesday, December 22, 2026 at 11 a.m. Wednesday, December 23, 2026 at 11 a.m. Sunday, December 27, 2026 at 11 a.m. California Theatre, San Jose, CA Concert Length Approx. 55 minutes No intermission Ballet performance with live orchestra New Ballet Dalia Rawson, choreographer Symphony San Jose Thomas Shoebotham, conductor Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky The Nutcracker (Act I) My Very First Nutcracker is a special one-act presentation of The San Jose Nutcracker ideal for families with toddlers, preschoolers, and young children. This joyful holiday production features the festive holiday party, at which Uncle Nikola reveals his fascinating gifts. Kids will marvel at the historic San Jose Electric Light Tower rising magically above the streets of San Jose, and cheer on adorable mice and toy soldiers who compete to win a magic crown. Introduce your family to the magic of classical ballet! Children aged one year and older require a ticket for entry. Pre-concert festivities occur one hour prior the concert. The fun begins with festive holiday decorations in the elegant lobby and holiday music played on the theatre’s historical organ. Attendees will enjoy opportunities to interact with costumed characters and be photographed in magical fairytale settings, plus enjoy treats and toys available for purchase. Concessions offer something for everyone, from sweet treats to celebratory beverages. Throughout the venue, a special play zone featuring two brick pits — one with DUPLO bricks and one with Soft Bricks provided by Legoland exclusively for My Very First Nutcracker — adds an extra touch of magic to the experience. The San Jose Nutcracker takes place in San Jose at the turn of the last century. This unique production features landmarks of the era, with dazzling new scenic elements including a growing replica of the historic San Jose Light Tower and a skyline of San Jose inspired by the city in 1905. Costumes for the first act were inspired by period dolls from the History San Jose archives and the second act was inspired by our valley in the last century, carpeted in orchard blossoms and known as “The Valley of Heart’s Delight.” Swirling snowflakes, waltzing flowers, and The Sugarplum Fairy will make this holiday ballet a new favorite for the entire family. Explore our seating map here. Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday: 12 p.m. – 4 p.m. Monday – Friday, 10am-5pm

title: My Very First Symphony
description: Our instrument petting zoo lets little hands explore real orchestral instruments up close.
parentSummary: Our instrument petting zoo lets little hands explore real orchestral instruments up close.
sourceDescriptionRaw: Sunday, March 7, 2027 at 11 a.m. California Theatre, San Jose, CA Concert Length Approx. 55 minutes No intermission $25 - Child $40 - Adult Monique Hafen Adams, narrator Symphony San Jose The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra My Very First Symphony is a special one-hour concert presented by Symphony San Jose featuring Britten’s The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, ideal for families with toddlers, preschoolers, and young children. Brilliantly inventive and endlessly engaging, Britten’s The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra takes listeners on a tour of the ensemble, revealing how the personality of each instrument and their respective families contribute to the symphonic sound. Introducing children to classical music opens a world of imagination, emotion, and discovery. Live orchestral performances captivate young minds with vibrant sounds, dynamic storytelling, and the magic of musicians creating music together in real time. These early experiences spark curiosity, build listening skills, and create lasting memories that can inspire a lifelong love of music and the arts. Children aged one year and older require a ticket for entry. No furry friends here—just something even better! Our instrument petting zoo lets little hands explore real orchestral instruments up close. Kids can touch a violin, tap on percussion, and discover the sounds that bring music to life. It’s a fun, interactive way to turn curious toddlers into engaged listeners before the concert even starts. Join us one hour prior to the concert and let the musical adventure begin! Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday: 12 p.m. – 4 p.m. Monday – Friday, 10am-5pm

title: Disney's Dare to Dream Jr.
description: As the trainees work together to discover their own dreams, they uncover the power that imagination and teamwork have to make anything possible.
parentSummary: As the trainees work together to discover their own dreams, they uncover the power that imagination and teamwork have to make anything possible.
sourceDescriptionRaw: | Performances: June 23-27 | Children's Musical Theater San Jose (CMT San Jose) presents Disney's Dare to Dream JR., a musical revue that follows an eager group of trainees on their first day at a fictional Walt Disney Imagineering Studio. As the trainees work together to discover their own dreams, they uncover the power that imagination and teamwork have to make anything possible. Celebrating 100 years of Disney music, the production features 20 songs spanning a century of beloved films, including selections making their stage debut alongside favorites from The Princess and the Frog, Coco, Encanto, and Frozen II. Now in its 59th season, CMT San Jose is one of the region's premier youth performing arts organizations, offering training and performance opportunities to thousands of young artists each year. CMT San Jose trains and educates today's youth through musical theater to set and achieve high artistic and personal goals, and to inspire them to become exemplary artists, patrons and citizens of tomorrow. The organization is dedicated to fostering creativity and a lifelong love of the performing arts in a supportive and inclusive environment.
